indicators.description:
The full indicator is: Number of gender-responsive, conflict-sensitive development institutions, policies, plans, or cross-border initiatives in place, with UN support, that promote and protect human rights, prevent systemic human rights violations to: 
a) Address conflict drivers; 
b) Strengthen social cohesion; 
c) Prevent risk of conflict, including climate security; and 
d) End all forms of violence, promote the rule of law, and ensure equal access to justice for all

The indicator measures the following:

UN support to Kenya in developing gender-responsive institutional and human capacities necessary to prevent, manage, or resolve conflicts. UN support is geared to build national capacities for conflict prevention, like convening multi-stakeholder dialogues to bridge significant gaps on critical national issues, and/or conducting advocacy for peace and social cohesion. Another example is through support to national and/or local formal or informal mechanisms that promote social cohesion and conflict prevention through collaborative planning, problem solving and leadership. Policies, plans and institutions can cut across a wide range of topics ranging from electoral process, conflicts over land and natural resources, to access to mainstream development and primary political and governance related reforms. Specific examples of institutions, policies and plans include: (NCTC, SDG, Interior defence, national police, gender policy, KNAP II, UWIANO Platform for Peace, Women Mediation Network-Kenya, AWLN-K, County Women Peace Committee Network)

•	UN helps countries establish and strengthen national peace infrastructure. This includes the processes, policies and institutions that design, support and enhance social resilience to violent conflict, and build sustainable freedom from strife. This indicator also measures UN support in boosting national and local capacities for peace and mediation. 

•	This indicator monitors the number of plans, policies and systems in place that promote social cohesion within humanitarian contexts through targeted UN recovery (disaster and conflict) programmes and interventions. Specifically, it also captures institutions, polices and plans that not only recognize gender inequalities and power imbalances, but also actively seek to address and mitigate these inequalities through interventions.

It measures at both national and county level, measurement is number

indicators.description:
This indicator estimates the number of countries that have measures to support and advance women’s leadership and participation in decision-making in six sectors: 
1) public institutions, 
2) elected positions including parliaments, 
3) judiciary, 
4) private sector, and 
5) mediation, reconciliation and peacebuilding mechanisms, and 
6) natural resource management. 

These measures entail normative, legal, and regulatory frameworks, national policies, programmes, plans, initiatives, legislative documents and regulations that directly serve to support and advance women’s leadership and equal participation, including through digital platforms. Specific examples of proven interventions include gender quotas, gender-responsive resource allocations, preferential treatment, targeted recruitment, hiring and promotion, and gender parity targets for task forces, standing committees and other decision-making bodies. Additional measures to advance women’s leadership and participation include collection and use of data disaggregated by gender, age, race/ethnicity and other factors, mentorship programmes and other capacity-building, training and awareness-raising initiatives. Measures to advance women’s participation and decision-making in the public sector have been applied in other sectors. For example, 10 countries have legislated quotas for women on corporate boards of publicly listed companies. Applying such approaches more systematically across sectors would contribute to the expansion of the pool of women candidates ready to take up decision-making positions in political, economic and public life. Advancing women’s leadership and participation in decision-making in natural resource management and climate resilient governance entails: promoting women’s equal engagement in local, regional, sectoral and national environment, climate and energy related planning processes; promoting women’s voice in decision-making and policy in global, national and local planning and decision-making bodies, e.g. local water management committees; supporting women’s engagement at leadership and/or decision making levels in producer organizations, cooperatives, labour unions, outgrow schemes, etc.; promoting women’s voice (including indigenous peoples and local community groups) in partnerships and alliances with regional and national networks; providing policy level training opportunities to help women participate in decision-making forums; and enhancing women’s decision-making capabilities around land, forests, water and other biological resources they use

Specific examples include: Implementation of the 2/3rds Gender Rule by national parliament and executive, Development and/or implementation of laws and policies related to election management, inclusive and peaceful election, Capacities  of elections management bodies (IEBC and ORPP) or National and County Assemblies to undertake gender responsive  legislation, representation and oversight 

National and county level disaggregation is required. The scale is:

indicators.title: Quality of free and universal birth registration service within civil registration and vital statistics, in accordance with international standards and best practices, supported by the UN
indicators.description:
This indicator measures to what extent a country has a birth registration system in place that is free and universal, and placed within the civil registration system. Universal birth registration is one of the most powerful instruments for ensuring equity over a broad scope of services and interventions for children. Birth registration within civil registration and vital statistics is central for ensuring that children are counted and have access to basic services such as health, social security and education. Knowing the age of children is critical to protecting them from: child labour; arrest and treatment as adults in the justice system; forcible conscription in armed forces; child marriage; and trafficking and sexual exploitation.
Output Indicator value –
• ‘Low’ refers to countries that fulfil 0 or 1 of the 6 criteria for a free and universal birth registration service;
• ‘Medium’ refers to countries that fulfil 3, 4 or 5 of these criteria;
• ‘High’ refers to countries with a high quality free and universal birth registration service by fulfilling all 6 criteria’
Six criteria for a free and universal birth registration service –
1. Birth registration is free for all children (0-17 years)
2. The first copy of birth certificate is issued free of charge for all children (0-17 years); if not so, specify period/age group for which it is provided free of charge
3. Birth registration is required by law for all births
4. Births are registered without discrimination.
5. Civil registration system is in place to reach all districts/sub-districts.
6. Civil registration records are kept permanently and retrievable from a secondary/back-up source and are secure.

indicators.title: Number of people with access to adequate housing, in accordance with international human rights standards, with UN’s support
indicators.description:
This indicator measures the a) the number people with increased access to affordable housing as a result of UN support b)number of people with increased access to urban basic services (Municipal Solid Waste Management, urban mobility, urban energy, WASH)  c) total number of people in adequate housing is measured by using the number of people living in slums/informal settlements and adding the number of people living in unaffordable housing. Integrating these two aspects makes the indicator universal as it helps capture housing conditions in both developed and developing countries thus addressing the fundamental principle of leaving no one behind (LNOB) as a result of UN support. Data will be collected for men, women, youth and PWDs.  For housing to be adequate, it must provide more than four walls and a roof, and at a minimum, meet the following criteria: 

1)        Legal security of tenure, which guarantees legal protection against forced evictions, harassment and other threats. 
2)        Availability of services, materials, facilities and infrastructure, including safe drinking water, adequate sanitation, energy for cooking, heating, lighting, food storage or refuse disposal. 
3)        Affordability, as housing is not adequate if its cost threatens or compromises the occupants’ enjoyment of other human rights. 
4)        Habitability, as housing is not adequate if it does not guarantee physical safety or provide adequate space, as well as protection against the cold, damp, heat, rain, wind, other threats to health and structural hazards.
5)        Accessibility, as housing is not adequate if the specific needs of disadvantaged and marginalized 
groups are not taken into account (such as the poor, people facing discrimination; persons with 
disabilities, victims of natural disasters); 
6)        Location, as housing is not adequate if it is cut off from employment opportunities, healthcare 
7)        services, schools, childcare centres, and other social facilities, or if located in dangerous or polluted sites or in immediate proximity to pollution sources; and
8)        Cultural adequacy, as housing is not adequate if it does not respect and consider the expression of cultural identity and ways of life.

a) Participatory; and b) Land efficient urban planning, with UN's support
indicators.description:
This indicator aims to measure government enhanced participatory and land efficient urban planning, with UN support. In participatory urban planning calls for the active engagement and inclusivity of all key stakeholders with particular attention to programmes and projects beneficiaries and vulnerable groups (number of stakeholders  and community members) integrated and actively engaging as part of the public participation throughout the planning process  during the preparation & development of different levels of plans at national and county governments' level. 

a) Participatory urban planning

The development of sustainable human settlements calls for active engagement of all key stakeholders with particular attention to programme beneficiaries and vulnerable groups. Therefore, local and national government should strive to: 
a) facilitate and protect people's participation and civic engagement through independent civil society organizations that can be from diverse backgrounds - local, national, and international;
b) promote civic and human rights education and training programmes to make urban residents aware of their rights and the changing roles of diverse women, men, and young women and men in urban settings;
c) remove the barriers that block participation of socially marginalized groups and promote non-discrimination and promote non-discrimination and full and equal participation of women, young men and women and marginalized groups

Land efficient urban planning 

Urban growth has resulted in low density and sprawling settlements in urban areas. This urban pattern leads to deterioration of living conditions and low densities, making it costly and inefficient to provide infrastructures and services. The promotion of sustainable land use, urban sprawl. Extension and infill of existing neighborhoods are strategies and initiatives to promote adequate density urban growth, alleviating urban sprawl and maximizing land efficiency. They provide a city with a spatial structure that can support socioeconomic and environmental sustainability. city extension and infill are needed to enable cities to accommodate  the expected urban growth sustainability.

indicators.title: Proportion of urban population with proper access to Municipal services in Solid Waste Management (SWM)
indicators.description:
The Indicator will measure the proposal of population  with access to Basic MSW collection services (Proportion of population who receive waste collection services that are either basic improved or full defined by the service ladder of MSW collection services. Municipal Solid Waste Management is waste generated from: households, commerce and trade, small businesses, office buildings and institutions (schools, hospitals, government buildings). It also includes bulky waste (e.g. white goods, old furniture, mattresses) and waste from selected municipal services, e.g. waste from park and garden maintenance, waste from street cleaning services (street sweepings, the content of litter containers, market cleansing waste), if managed as waste. The definition excludes waste from municipal sewage network and treatment, municipal construction and demolition waste. The proportion of the population with Access to Basic Municipal Solid Waste (MSW) collection services is the proportion of the population who receive waste collection services that are either basic, improved or full, defined by the service ladder of MSW collection service. It considers aspects of frequency, regularity and proximity of the collection points
 
Ladder of MSW collection service that household receives (This aspect is measured under the SDG indicator 11.6.1 assessment but it is reported through a different indicator, SDG 1.4.1. on access to basic services).

SERVICE LEVEL                     DEFINITION
Full                                           - Receiving door-to-door MSW collection service with basic frequency and regularity and MSW is collected in three or more separate 
                                                       fractions; or 
                                                  - Having a designated collection point within 200m distance served with basic frequency and regularity and without major littering and 
                                                     MSW is collected in three or more separate fractions

Improved        - Receiving door-to-door MSW collection service with basic frequency and regularity and MSW is collected in a minimum of two, 
                            separate fractions (e.g. wet and dry fractions) 
                          - Having a designated collection point within 200m distance served with basic frequency and regularity and without major littering and 
                            MSW is collected in a minimum of two, separate fractions (e.g. wet and dry fractions)
Basic                - Receiving door-to-door MSW collection service with basic frequency and regularity or o Having designated collection point within 200m         
                            distance served with basic frequency and regularity
Limited              - Receiving door-to-door MSW collection service without basic frequency and regularity; o Having a designated collection point within 200m distance 
                             but not served with basic frequency and regularity; or o Having designated collection point in further than 200 m distance.
No                       - Receiving no waste collection service

NB: Basic frequency and regularity: served at least once a week for one year

indicators.description: Red List Index (RLI) measures overall trends in extinction risk for sets of species, based on genuine changes in their status over time. This indicator (RLI) measures changes in the overall conservation status of groups of species or entire ecosystems over time. The measurement helps in tracking trends in biodiversity and assessing the effectiveness of conservation efforts.  The Red List Index (RLI) is a metric used to assess the overall conservation status and trends of species around the world. It is a key component of the Red List of Threatened Species, which is maintained by the International Union for Conservation of Nature (IUCN). The Red List is a comprehensive database that categorizes species into various threat categories based on their risk of extinction. The RLI is typically calculated for a specific taxonomic group, such as birds, mammals, amphibians, or plants, and it can also be calculated for broader ecosystems.

indicators.description: This indicator monitors the Percentage of people living with HIV on ART in Kenya, disaggregated by age, gender, and ASAL Counties.  It is the 2nd 95 in the 95-95-95 cascade and UNAIDS targets where 95% of all people identified as HIV positive are put on ART by 2030. The numerator for the indicator is the number of people put on ART at any given point, mainly from KHIS, whereas the denominator is the estimated number of people living with HIV in Kenya, from the UNAIDS HIV estimates.

indicators.title: Mo Ibrahim Index of African Governance
indicators.description:
The Ibrahim Index of African Governance (IIAG) is an annually published composite index that provides a statistical measure of governance performance in African countries.

Governance is defined by the Mo Ibrahim Foundation as the provision of the political, social and economic public goods and services that a citizen has the right to expect from his or her state, and that a state has the responsibility to deliver to its citizens. This definition is focused on outputs and outcomes of policy. The IIAG governance framework comprises four dimensions (categories):

Safety & Rule of Law
Participation & Human Rights
Sustainable Economic Opportunity
Human Development
These categories are made up of 14 sub-categories, consisting of over 100 indicators. The latest IIAG is calculated using data from more than 30 independent sources.

Annual refinements are made to the IIAG, which may be methodological, or based on the inclusion or exclusion of indicators. The entire IIAG data set is therefore retrospectively revised, in accordance with best practices. Comparisons between years should therefore be performed entirely on the 2013 IIAG data set.

indicators.title: Whether or not legal, policy, institutional and practice frameworks are in place, operational and funded to promote, enforce and monitor equality and non-discrimination on the basis prohibited grounds in the constitution.
indicators.description:
The indicator will cover four areas of disaggregation:
Legal frameworks, policies, institutional frameworks and budgetary allocations to the selected institutions.
The indicator measures the establishment of institutions through constitutional and legislative means to promote, enforce and monitor human rights and gender equality and to ensure the principle of non-discrimination is embedded into the mandates of institutions. 
The indicator will also measure the extent to which policies, allocation of budgets and administrative processes of the institutions promote human rights and gender equality and are responsive to different needs and priorities of all persons in development, humanitarian and other sectors prioritized by the Country. 

Under reporting, county level frameworks and gender-responsiveness will be covered. LNOB disaggregation not relevant. It will be measured through a scale 0=not in place, 
1=work started 
2=work in progress
3=work almost complete 
4= in place
